newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Virgin says interested in SAA privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Virgin says interested in SAA privatisation.

text.p: British airline Virgin Atlantic said on Tuesday it would be interested in making a bid for a majority stake in any future privatisation of South Africa's national flag carrier South African Airways.

"We recently pulled out of the bidding for Sun Air. We'll be looking towards an alternative source of investment in South Africa which will probably mean South African Airways, as and when the privatisation comes up," Virgin general manager for southern Africa David James told Reuters.

Virgin Atlantic, which unveiled a new logo on Monday, announced its withdrawal last month from the Sun Air race, leaving three consortia bids accepted by the South African Ministry of Transport for the 100 percent sale of the airline.
The South Africa government announced in May it was likely to sell a strategic equity stake in SAA during 1998.
British Airways Plc and Deutsche Lufthansa AG are among companies to have expressed interest in acquiring a stake in SAA.
Virgin's James said the airline would look to be part of a consortium which aimed to snare a majority stake in the SAA privatisation, the size of which is yet to be decided.
"If you look at (Virgin Group Chief Executive) Richard Branson's track record it would be sensible to surmise that he'd be looking for a majority stake... in other words, 51 percent.
"I think we would probably want to do it as part of a consortium with some local black partners," he added.
James said it remained unclear to Virgin as to what proportion of SAA would eventually be sold off by the government.

"The most talked about scenario seems to be that the initial tranche would be 25 percent of SAA. I suspect that something else might happen. It could be that they sell the whole thing at once or perhaps retain a small shareholding for future black empowerment,"
"There is a possibility that the airline could be split into international and domestic and sold that way. It's difficult to tell at this stage but whatever happens, we're interested."
SAA, which registered a loss in the 1996/97 financial year, is in the process of restructuring which is expected to be completed in 1998.
James said Virgin was strengthening its presence in South Africa by moving to daily flights between London and Johannesburg from July 15.

"We started with three flights a week only in October, we doubled that in March. Now we're going daily and this is within nine months of starting the operation which is really quite something," he added.
The London-Johannesburg route was Virgin's most successful new operation since the airline first took to the air in 1984, James said.
The airline also was considering running direct flights from London to Cape Town to match existing services offered by British Airways and SAA, James said.
"It would be sensible for us to operate our own services into Cape Town as well and at some point in the near future we'll be looking very seriously at doing that," he said.
